title: 15. System Design Case Studies: Design Twitter / X
summary: Design Twitter / X — a microblogging and social-networking platform with ~300 M monthly active users, ~500 M tweets / day, asymmetric follow graph, personalized home timelines, trending topics, and tweet storms (threads).
objectives: Step 3: Deep Dive — Data Model (10 min)
Step 4: Deep Dive — Key Algorithms & APIs (10 min)

sections.title: Step 1: Clarify Requirements (5 min)
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Design Twitter / X — a microblogging and social-networking platform with ~300 M monthly active users, ~500 M tweets / day, asymmetric follow graph, personalized home timelines, trending topics, and tweet storms (threads). Focus on the **hybrid fanout timeline-generation algorithm** (fanout-on-write for normal users, fanout-on-read for celebrities), **tweet storage on Cassandra**, **timeline caching in Redis**, and **trending topics via sliding-window counting**. ---

### Functional Requirements
- **Tweet**: post ≤ 280 chars (140 before 2017), with optional media (photo / video / GIF ≤ 5 items, video ≤ 2 min 20 s), location, and poll. Replies, quote tweets, retweets (native + quote).
- **Follow / unfollow**: asymmetric — A following B does not imply B following A.
- **Home timeline**: reverse-chronological + ranked mix of tweets from followed users + recommended tweets.
- **User timeline**: profile page showing a user's own tweets, replies, media, likes.
- **Search**: full-text over tweets, by hashtag, @mention, keyword; with recency ranking.
- **Trending topics**: top-N hashtags/keywords in the last 24 h, personalized by location/who-you-follow.
- **Notifications**: likes, retweets, follows, mentions, DMs.
- **Direct messages** (simplified — full DM = WhatsApp design): 1:1 and small-group messages.
- **Tweet storm**: a numbered thread of related tweets by the same author.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- **Availability** 99.99 % for timeline reads (≈ 52 min downtime / year) — the visible feature.
- **Latency**: timeline generation p99 < 200 ms (cached), tweet post p99 < 1 s.
- **Scale**: 300 M MAU, ~150 M DAU, ~500 M tweets/day, ~5 B timeline reads/day (≈ 60 k reads/s avg, ~150 k/s peak).
- **Durability**: tweets never lost (deleted tweets also retained for grace period for analytics / appeals).
- **Consistency**: eventual consistency acceptable for counts; strong consistency for tweet visibility (a posted tweet must be readable by the author immediately).

### Back-of-Envelope Estimation
- **Tweet writes**: 500 M / 86 400 ≈ 5 800 tweets/s avg, ~3× peak during live events ≈ 17 k/s.
- **Timeline reads**: 5 B / 86 400 ≈ 60 k reads/s avg, peak ~150 k/s.
- **Fanout amplification**: average user has 100 followers → 5 800 × 100 = 580 k feed updates/s. Celebrity tweet (Justin Bieber, 100 M followers) → 100 M feed pushes — this is exactly the problem that pushes us toward **hybrid fanout**.
- **Tweet storage**: 500 M tweets/day × 500 bytes avg (text + metadata, excluding media) × 5 years = 460 TB. Media: 500 M × 20 % × 1 MB = 100 TB/day → 180 PB / 5 years.
- **Timeline cache**: 150 M DAU × 1 KB cached feed list = 150 GB in Redis (replicated 3× = 450 GB).
- **Network egress**: 60 k reads/s × 50 KB per page = 3 GB/s = 24 Tbps across regions.

### Scope
In scope: tweet posting, timeline generation (home + user), follow graph, retweet/quote, search, trending topics, tweet storms. Out of scope: full DM system (covered in WhatsApp design), ML-based recommendation ranking (covered in Instagram / Facebook News Feed), live video / Spaces audio (covered in YouTube Live), ad serving.

sections.title: Step 2: High-Level Architecture (10 min)
sections.body:
### Components 1. **Edge / CDN** (CloudFront / Akamai): cache media assets, terminate TLS, route API calls to nearest regional cluster. 2. **API Gateway** (Kong / Envoy): rate limit (token bucket per user + global), auth (OAuth 2.0 + bearer JWT), request routing. 3. **Tweet Service**: receives new tweets, persists to Cassandra, publishes a `tweet-created` Kafka event. 4. **Timeline Service** (read path): serves home and user timelines; reads from Redis feed cache, falls back to on-read fanout for celeb follows. 5. **Fanout Worker**: consumes `tweet-created`, iterates poster's followers, LPUSHes tweet ID into each follower's Redis feed list. Skips celebrities (fanout-on-read). 6. **User Graph Service**: Postgres-sharded `follows` table; lookups: `followers(user_id)` and `following(user_id)`. 7. **Search Service**: Elasticsearch / Lucene inverted index over tweet text + hashtags + mentions, with BM25 + recency boost. 8. **Trending Service**: stream processing over tweet hashtags/keywords, sliding 1-min / 5-min / 24-h windows, top-N per region. 9. **Notification Service**: emits push notifications for mentions, likes, follows, DMs. 10. **Media Service**: S3 presigned uploads → transcoder → CDN. 11. **Cassandra** cluster: `tweets`, `user_tweets`, `home_tweets` (pre-materialized), counters. 12. **Redis** cluster: `feed:{user_id}` lists (timeline cache), `user_tweets:{user_id}` lists, presence / locks. 13. **Kafka** event bus: `tweet-created`, `tweet-deleted`, `like`, `retweet`, `follow`. ### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD Client[Mobile / Web Client] --> CDN[Edge CDN] CDN --> GW[API Gateway
Kong + OAuth2] GW --> TS[Tweet Service] GW --> TL[Timeline Service] GW --> SS[Search Service] GW --> TR[Trending Service] GW --> US[User Graph Service] TS --> CASS1[(Cassandra: tweets,
user_tweets, counters)] TS --> K1[(Kafka: tweet-created)] K1 --> FW[Fanout Worker] FW --> UGS[User Graph
followers lookup] FW --> RC[(Redis: feed:user_id
cached timelines)] TL --> RC TL --> CASS2[(Cassandra: home_tweets
for celeb pull)] SS --> ES[(Elasticsearch
inverted index)] TR --> K2[(Kafka: hashtags stream)] TR --> RS[(Redis: top-N
per region)] US --> PG[(Postgres sharded
follows table)] TS --> S3[(S3 + CDN: media)] style FW fill:#ffe4b5 style TL fill:#b5ffe4 style RC fill:#ffd5d5 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ | Mobile / | | Edge | | API | | Web App |----->| CDN |----->| Gateway | +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----+-----+ | rate-limit + auth +---------------------------------+--------------------------+ | | | v v v +---------------+ +---------------+ +---------------+ | Tweet Service | | Timeline Svc | | User Graph | | (write) | | (read) | | Service | +-------+-------+ +-------+-------+ +-------+-------+ | | | | persists | reads | reads v v v +---------------+ +---------------+ +---------------+ | Cassandra | | Redis | | Postgres | | tweets, | | feed:{u} | | follows | | user_tweets, | | (cached | | (sharded by | | counters | | timelines) | | followee_id)| +-------+-------+ +-------+-------+ +---------------+ | ^ | publishes | v | +---------------+ followers +-----------------+ | Kafka |---> lookup --->| Fanout Worker | | tweet-created | | (skip celebs > | +-------+-------+ | 100K followers)| | +-----------------+ v +---------------+ stream +-----------------+ | Trending |<-------------| Kafka topic | | Service | hashtags | hashtags | +-------+-------+ +-----------------+ | v +---------------+ | Redis top-N | | per region | +---------------+ ``` ### Request Flow Walkthrough 1. **Post a tweet**: Client → CDN → API Gateway (auth + rate-limit) → Tweet Service. Tweet Service validates content, allocates Snowflake tweet ID, writes to Cassandra `tweets` and `user_tweets`, enqueues media transcoding if needed, publishes `tweet-created` event to Kafka. Returns the new tweet ID immediately to the client. 2. **Fanout-on-write**: Fanout Worker consumes `tweet-created`, calls User Graph Service to fetch the poster's followers. If `follower_count < 100 k`, iterate followers and `LPUSH feed:{follower_id} tweet_id` into Redis (list capped at ~800). For celebrities, skip — those tweets will be pulled on read. 3. **Read home timeline**: Client → Timeline Service. Service fetches `feed:{user_id}` from Redis (the pre-computed list), fetches recent tweets from any celeb follows (those that were skipped during fanout-on-write), merges and de-dupes, hydrates tweet objects from Cassandra, applies ML ranking for the "recommended" mix, returns top 20. 4. **Trending**: A Flink job continuously consumes the `hashtags` Kafka topic, maintains a sliding-window count per hashtag per region in Redis, and serves top-N via `ZRANGE trending:{region}:{window} 0 9 REV`.

sections.title: Step 3: Deep Dive — Data Model (10 min)
sections.body:
### Tables / Schema

**Cassandra — `tweets`** (one row per tweet)
```sql
CREATE TABLE tweets (
    tweet_id      timeuuid,        -- Snowflake-encoded
    user_id       bigint,
    text          text,
    media_ids     list<uuid>,
    reply_to      timeuuid,        -- null unless reply
    quote_of      timeuuid,        -- null unless quote tweet
    retweet_of    timeuuid,        -- null unless retweet
    created_at    timestamp,
    location      text,
    PRIMARY KEY (tweet_id)
);
```

**Cassandra — `user_tweets`** (a user's own tweets, ordered by time)
```sql
CREATE TABLE user_tweets (
    user_id     bigint,
    created_at  timestamp,
    tweet_id    timeuuid,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, created_at, tweet_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (created_at DESC, tweet_id DESC);
```

**Cassandra — `home_tweets`** (pre-materialized timeline for celeb-read path, optional)
```sql
CREATE TABLE home_tweets (
    user_id     bigint,            -- the reader
    created_at  timestamp,
    tweet_id    timeuuid,
    poster_id   bigint,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, created_at, tweet_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (created_at DESC, tweet_id DESC);
```

**Cassandra — `tweet_counts`** (counters for likes/retweets/replies)
```sql
CREATE TABLE tweet_counts (
    tweet_id    timeuuid,
    likes       counter,
    retweets    counter,
    replies     counter,
    PRIMARY KEY (tweet_id)
);
```

**Postgres (sharded by `followee_id`) — `follows`**
```sql
CREATE TABLE follows (
    follower_id  bigint NOT NULL,
    followee_id  bigint NOT NULL,
    created_at   timestamptz DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (followee_id, follower_id)   -- partition by followee_id (fanout lookup)
);
CREATE INDEX ON follows (follower_id);       -- "who do I follow"
CREATE TABLE users (
    user_id     bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    username    text UNIQUE,
    display     text,
    bio         text,
    follower_count  bigint DEFAULT 0,
    following_count bigint DEFAULT 0
);
```

**Redis**
```
LIST  feed:{user_id}                 # pre-computed timeline (tweet IDs), capped ~800
LIST  user_tweets:{user_id}          # the user's recent tweet IDs
ZSET  trending:{region}:{window}     # hashtag -> count, sliding window
KV    rate:{user_id}:{endpoint}      # token-bucket state for rate limit
KV    tweet_lock:{tweet_id}          # short-lived lock for edit window
```

### Indexes
- Cassandra PK `tweet_id` → O(1) tweet lookup.
- `user_tweets` partitioned by `user_id` with reverse clustering by `created_at` → user profile reads are O(limit).
- `home_tweets` partitioned by reader's `user_id` → fast timeline reads even without Redis (fallback).
- Postgres index on `follows (follower_id)` for "who do I follow" (profile page).
- Elasticsearch inverted index over `text`, `hashtags`, `mentions` for search.

### Storage Choice
- **Cassandra** for tweets, user_tweets, home_tweets, counters: write-heavy, time-ordered, linearly scalable. Twitter actually migrated primary tweet storage from MySQL to Cassandra in 2010 for exactly this reason — Cassandra's LSM-tree writes and automatic sharding handled the 5 800 tweets/s sustained write rate that MySQL replication could not.
- **PostgreSQL (sharded by followee_id)** for the follow graph: ACID guarantees for follow/unfollow (a half-committed follow is a bug). Partitioning by `followee_id` co-locates all followers of one user on a single shard — perfect for the fanout lookup.
- **Redis** for the timeline cache: in-memory list ops (LPUSH / LRANGE) take < 1 ms, and the cache absorbs the 60 k reads/s traffic that Cassandra alone could not serve at p99 < 200 ms.
- **Elasticsearch** for tweet search: inverted index with BM25 + recency boost.
- **S3 + CDN** for media (photos, videos, GIFs).

sections.title: Step 4: Deep Dive — Key Algorithms & APIs (10 min)
sections.body:
### API Design
```
POST /api/v1/tweets
  body: { "text": "...", "media_ids": ["..."], "reply_to": "...", "quote_of": "..." }
  resp: { "tweet_id": "...", "created_at": "..." }

GET  /api/v1/tweets/{id}

DELETE /api/v1/tweets/{id}

POST /api/v1/tweets/{id}/retweet
DELETE /api/v1/tweets/{id}/retweet

GET  /api/v1/timeline/home?cursor=...&limit=20
GET  /api/v1/timeline/user/{user_id}?cursor=...&limit=20

POST /api/v1/users/{id}/follow
DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}/follow

GET  /api/v1/search?q=...&type=latest&cursor=...

GET  /api/v1/trending?location=US&window=24h

POST /api/v1/tweetstorm    # create a thread
  body: { "tweets": [ {"text":"1/ "}, {"text":"2/ "}, ... ] }
  resp: { "thread_id": "...", "tweet_ids": ["...","..."] }
```

### Key Algorithms

**1. Snowflake tweet ID.** Each tweet ID encodes: timestamp (ms since epoch, 41 bits) + machine/shard ID (10 bits) + per-ms sequence (12 bits). The ID is monotonically increasing and sortable by time — so `ORDER BY tweet_id DESC` == `ORDER BY created_at DESC`, and we can paginate timelines with `WHERE tweet_id < ?` instead of a separate cursor column. Twitter open-sourced this in 2010; the same pattern is used by Instagram, Discord, and many others.

**2. Hybrid fanout — the core algorithm.** When a tweet is created:
- Fetch follower set for the poster. If `count < 100 k` (normal user), iterate and `LPUSH feed:{follower_id} tweet_id` in batches of ~1 000 per Redis pipeline. Cap each feed list at ~800 entries (older tweets evicted). Read path: one `LRANGE feed:{user_id} 0 19` returns 20 IDs in < 1 ms.
- If `count >= 100 k` (celebrity), **skip fanout**. At read time, Timeline Service detects celeb follows and pulls their recent `user_tweets` directly, merging into the cached timeline.
- Why 100 k? Below this, fanout-on-write is cheap (one Redis pipeline of 100 k LPUSHes ≈ 50 ms). Above it, fanout becomes wasteful — most of those 100 k feeds get an entry that's never read or scrolled past, plus the write latency balloons. Twitter reportedly used a similar threshold (~75 k in 2012, later tuned).

**3. Timeline read merge.** For a given reader:
```
cached = LRANGE feed:{reader} 0 199        # ~200 cached IDs
for celeb in celeb_follows(reader):
    cached += LRANGE user_tweets:{celeb} 0 9   # recent 10 celeb tweets
candidates = hydrate_and_dedupe(cached)    # fetch full tweet objects from Cassandra
ranked = ml_ranker.rank(candidates, reader) # optional: ranked mix
return ranked[0:20]
```

**4. Trending topics.** A Flink job consumes the `hashtags` Kafka topic (every tweet emits one event per hashtag). It maintains in Redis a sliding-window counter per `(hashtag, region, window)` using a **GenMill-style bucketed approach**: keep 60 one-minute buckets (covering 1 h) and a 24 h aggregate. Top-N served via `ZREVRANGEBYSCORE trending:US:24h +inf -inf LIMIT 0 10`. To avoid spam / coordinated manipulation, ignore hashtags from accounts younger than 30 days, dedupe by IP / device fingerprint, and apply minimum-volume threshold (e.g., 1 000 mentions in window).

**5. Tweet storm (thread).** A thread is posted atomically: the client sends N tweets; the Tweet Service inserts each in turn, linking each `reply_to` to the previous one's `tweet_id`, and tags all with a `thread_id` Snowflake. Reading the thread = `SELECT * FROM tweets WHERE thread_id = ? ORDER BY tweet_id`. This is what allows "Show this thread" to expand the whole sequence.

**6. Read-after-write consistency.** When a user posts a tweet, their own timeline must show it immediately (otherwise the user thinks the post failed). Trick: Timeline Service **prepends the just-posted tweet_id to the user's own feed list before fanout completes**, so a subsequent `GET /timeline/home` returns it instantly. For other users, eventual consistency (1–5 s) is acceptable.

**7. Edit Tweet (X, 2022).** Edits create a new version row `tweet_versions (tweet_id, version, text, edited_at)`; the original tweet row keeps `current_version` pointer. Timeline cache holds the tweet_id, not the content, so edits propagate on next hydrate. Versions are visible for 30 min after posting (Twitter's actual policy).

```python
# twitter_timeline.py — hybrid fanout with Snowflake IDs and celeb pull-on-read
import time, threading, hashlib
from collections import defaultdict, deque

EPOCH = 1_288_834_974_657   # Twitter's real Snowflake epoch (Nov 4, 2010, 01:42:54.657 UTC)
class Snowflake:
    def __init__(self, machine_id):
        self.mid, self.seq, self.last, self.l = machine_id, 0, -1, threading.Lock()
    def next(self):
        with self.l:
            ts = int(time.time() * 1000) - EPOCH
            if ts == self.last:
                self.seq = (self.seq + 1) & 0xFFF
                if self.seq == 0:
                    while ts <= self.last: ts = int(time.time() * 1000) - EPOCH
            else:
                self.seq = 0
            self.last = ts
            return (ts << 22) | (self.mid << 10) | self.seq
    @staticmethod
    def ts(id_): return (id_ >> 22) + EPOCH

CELEB_THRESHOLD = 100_000
FEED_CAP = 800

class Tweet:
    def __init__(self, tweet_id, user_id, text, ts=None):
        self.id, self.user_id, self.text = tweet_id, user_id, text
        self.ts = ts or Snowflake.ts(tweet_id)
        self.like_count, self.retweet_count = 0, 0

class RedisMock:
    def __init__(self): self.kv = {}
    def lpush(self, k, *vs):
        d = self.kv.setdefault(k, deque(maxlen=FEED_CAP))
        for v in vs: d.appendleft(v)
    def lrange(self, k, s, e):
        v = list(self.kv.get(k, []))
        return v[s:e] if e != -1 else v[s:]
    def zadd(self, k, member, score):
        z = self.kv.setdefault(k, {})
        z[member] = max(z.get(member, 0), score)
    def zrevrange(self, k, n):
        z = self.kv.get(k, {})
        return [m for m, _ in sorted(z.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])[:n]]

class CassandraMock:
    def __init__(self):
        self.tweets = {}
        self.user_tweets = defaultdict(list)        # user_id -> [tweet_id,...] desc
        self.followers = defaultdict(set)           # followee_id -> set(follower_id)
        self.following = defaultdict(set)           # follower_id -> set(followee_id)
    def add_tweet(self, t):
        self.tweets[t.id] = t
        self.user_tweets[t.user_id].insert(0, t.id)  # keep desc by ts

class FanoutWorker:
    def __init__(self, cass, redis): self.c, self.r = cass, redis
    def on_tweet(self, t):
        followers = self.c.followers.get(t.user_id, set())
        if len(followers) > CELEB_THRESHOLD:
            print(f"  [skip] @{t.user_id} has {len(followers)} followers -> on-read pull")
            return
        # batched LPUSH via pipeline (mocked as loop)
        for f in followers:
            self.r.lpush(f"feed:{f}", t.id)
        # author's own timeline: prepend immediately for read-after-write
        self.r.lpush(f"feed:{t.user_id}", t.id)
        print(f"  [fanout] @{t.user_id} -> {len(followers)+1} feeds updated")

class TimelineService:
    def __init__(self, cass, redis): self.c, self.r = cass, redis
    def home(self, user_id, limit=20):
        candidates = list(self.r.lrange(f"feed:{user_id}", 0, 199))
        # pull celeb follows on-read
        for celeb in self.c.following.get(user_id, set()):
            if len(self.c.followers.get(celeb, set())) > CELEB_THRESHOLD:
                candidates += self.r.lrange(f"user_tweets:{celeb}", 0, 9)
        # hydrate + dedupe
        seen, out = set(), []
        for tid in candidates:
            if tid in seen: continue
            seen.add(tid)
            t = self.c.tweets.get(tid)
            if t: out.append(t)
            if len(out) >= limit: break
        return out

class TrendingService:
    def __init__(self, redis): self.r = redis
    def on_tweet(self, t, hashtags):
        for tag in hashtags:
            self.r.zadd("trending:global:24h", tag, 1)
    def top(self, n=10):
        return self.r.zrevrange("trending:global:24h", n)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cass, redis = CassandraMock(), RedisMock()
    snow = Snowflake(machine_id=1)
    fanout = FanoutWorker(cass, redis)
    tl = TimelineService(cass, redis)
    trending = TrendingService(redis)

    # Bob: normal user with 50 followers
    bob = 1
    for i in range(50): cass.followers[bob].add(1000+i); cass.following[1000+i].add(bob)
    # Katy: celebrity with 1.2M followers
    katy = 2
    for i in range(1_200_000): cass.followers[katy].add(2000+i)
    # Alice follows both
    alice = 999
    cass.following[alice].add(bob); cass.following[alice].add(katy)
    cass.followers[bob].add(alice); cass.followers[katy].add(alice)
    # seed user_tweets list (mock) for katy
    for _ in range(3):
        tid = snow.next()
        cass.add_tweet(Tweet(tid, katy, "old celeb tweet"))
        redis.lpush(f"user_tweets:{katy}", tid)

    # Bob tweets -> fanout-on-write
    t1 = Tweet(snow.next(), bob, "morning coffee #coffee #sf")
    cass.add_tweet(t1)
    fanout.on_tweet(t1)
    redis.lpush(f"user_tweets:{bob}", t1.id)
    trending.on_tweet(t1, ["coffee", "sf"])

    # Katy tweets -> skip fanout
    t2 = Tweet(snow.next(), katy, "new album out! #music")
    cass.add_tweet(t2)
    fanout.on_tweet(t2)
    redis.lpush(f"user_tweets:{katy}", t2.id)
    trending.on_tweet(t2, ["music"])

    # Alice reads her timeline
    print("\n[Alice's home timeline]")
    for t in tl.home(alice):
        print(f"  @{t.user_id}: {t.text}")

    print("\n[Trending topics]")
    print(" ", trending.top(5))
```

Running this script produces output showing Bob's tweet was fanned out to Alice's feed (and his own), Katy's tweet was skipped during fanout but pulled into Alice's timeline on-read, and the trending list contains `coffee`, `sf`, `music`.

sections.title: Step 5: Scalability & Reliability (5 min)
sections.body:
### Scaling Challenges
- **Fanout amplification**: One celeb tweet → 100 M Redis writes if we fanout-on-write naively. The 100 k threshold caps the worst case to ~100 k writes per tweet, but with thousands of celebs tweeting per minute the sustained rate is still high. Mitigation: pipeline batches of 1 000 LPUSHes per Redis round-trip, shard Redis by feed hash slot, and skip inactive followers (no app-open in 30 days) — Twitter's "fanout-on-write with skip" optimization reportedly cut write volume ~40 %.
- **Cache size**: 150 M DAU × 1 KB feed = 150 GB hot set. Redis Cluster shards this across ~30 nodes (5 GB / node). Each shard is 3× replicated for HA.
- **Read spikes during live events**: World Cup final, election nights, Apple keynote. A single celeb tweet can cause a 100× read spike on a few hot Redis slots. Mitigation: read-through fallback to Cassandra `home_tweets`, request coalescing (multiple concurrent requests for the same feed collapse into one Redis read), and 1 s client-side caching.
- **Cassandra write hotspots**: If all tweets hit one partition (e.g., the same `user_id`), that node overheats. Mitigation: tweets are partitioned by `tweet_id` (not `user_id`) in the `tweets` table, spreading writes evenly. `user_tweets` is partitioned by `user_id`, but a single user's write rate is naturally low (avg 1 tweet/day); only super-posting celebs are a concern, and they're rare.
- **Trending manipulation**: Hashtag brigading, botnets, coordinated spam. Mitigation: only count hashtags from accounts > 30 days old, dedupe by device fingerprint, volume + velocity anomaly detection, manual allow-list for known campaigns.

### Caching Strategy
- **L1 (client)**: 1 s in-memory cache of timeline to dedupe rapid refreshes.
- **L2 (CDN)**: media assets and immutable API responses (user profile, tweet by ID) cached 60 s.
- **L3 (Redis)**: pre-computed `feed:{user_id}` lists, hot tweet objects (LRU 10 M entries), `user_tweets:{user_id}`.
- **L4 (Cassandra)**: source of truth, with row cache for hot tweets.
- **Cache invalidation**: tweet deletion publishes `tweet-deleted` → Fanout Worker iterates followers and `LREM feed:{follower_id} 1 deleted_tweet_id` (best-effort). Deletes are rare vs reads, so this is fine.

### Failure Modes
- **Redis cluster partial outage**: timeline reads fall back to Cassandra `home_tweets` (pre-materialized) + on-the-fly celeb pull. Reads are slower (p99 ~800 ms instead of 200 ms) but still serve.
- **Cassandra write failure**: Tweet Service retries with exponential backoff. If a quorum write fails, the API returns 5xx and the client retries. Snowflake IDs are idempotent (client can retry with same ID) so no duplicates.
- **Fanout worker backlog**: If Kafka lag grows (e.g., during a viral event), followers see tweets late. Mitigation: auto-scale workers based on lag, prioritize celeb-skip so their tweets are always available via on-read pull.
- **Snowflake clock skew**: If a worker's clock is wrong, IDs can collide or be out of order. Mitigation: NTP with bounded drift; Snowflake refuses to generate if clock has moved backwards.
- **Region failover**: Multi-region active-active with Cassandra multi-DC replication (LOCAL_QUORUM writes, reads from local DC). If one region goes down, Route 53 shifts traffic to the other; users see ~1 min of read staleness.
